title: Check if a string is a palindrome using streams.
shortTitle: Check if a string is a palindrome using streams

s1_definition.profdef: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Using `IntStream.range(0, n/2)` you compare the character at each position with its mirror from the end; if all pairs match, the string is a palindrome.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya folds the code in half and checks that the first letter matches the last, the second matches the second-last, and so on. If every mirrored pair agrees, it is a palindrome.
s1_definition.oneliner: `IntStream.range(0, n/2).allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n-1-i))` tests a palindrome.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Using `IntStream.range(0, n/2)` you compare the character at each position with its mirror from the end; if all pairs match, the string is a palindrome.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya folds the code in half and checks that the first letter matches the last, the second matches the second-last, and so on. If every mirrored pair agrees, it is a palindrome.

**One line to remember:** `IntStream.range(0, n/2).allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n-1-i))` tests a palindrome.

sections.s2_technical:
With `n = s.length()`, `IntStream.range(0, n / 2)` yields the indices of the first half. For each index i you check `s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n - 1 - i)`, comparing a character with its mirror. `allMatch` returns true only if every pair matches, and it short-circuits — the first mismatch returns false immediately without checking the rest.

You only iterate half the string because once the first half matches the mirrored second half, the whole string is confirmed. A single middle character in an odd-length string needs no check since it mirrors itself. This is efficient and avoids building a reversed copy.

The senior nuance is normalisation: real palindrome checks often ignore case, spaces, and punctuation, so I pre-process the string with something like lowercasing and stripping non-letters before the index comparison. The index-and-allMatch approach is more efficient than reversing the whole string and comparing, because it short-circuits and allocates nothing. I also treat empty and single-character strings as palindromes, which the half-range check handles naturally.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A validation routine at the National Bank of India flags reference codes that are palindromes, which are disallowed as too predictable.

This is exactly what the mirrored-index allMatch check does — it confirms whether the code reads the same both ways efficiently.

The code defines a `PalindromeService.isPalindrome` method and a demo.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: "madam", "SAV2001", and "Nurses run".

Step 1: For "madam", normalisation leaves it unchanged with length five, so the range covers indices zero and one.

Step 2: Index zero compares m with the last m, index one compares a with the second-last a, both match, and the middle d is skipped.

Step 3: allMatch returns true, so "madam" is a palindrome.

Step 4: "SAV2001" fails at the first mirrored pair; "Nurses run" normalises to "nursesrun" which reversed is "nurserun" — the pairs do not all match, so it is false in this spelling.

```
INFO: madam     → true
INFO: SAV2001   → false
INFO: Nurses run→ false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  "madam" (n=5)
    │ IntStream.range(0, 2)   ← first half
    │ i=0: s[0]=m == s[4]=m ✓
    │ i=1: s[1]=a == s[3]=a ✓   (middle s[2]=d skipped)
    │ allMatch → true
    ▼
  palindrome = true
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — palindrome via IntStream ═══

  ┌─ mirrored comparison ──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ n = length; IntStream.range(0, n/2) → first-half indices    │
  │ allMatch(i -> s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(n-1-i))              │
  │ short-circuits on first mismatch → efficient               │
  │ half the work; middle char self-mirrors (odd length)       │
  │ normalise first (lowercase, strip non-alphanumerics)       │
  │ empty/single char → vacuously true                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        PalindromeService      │
  │  + isPalindrome(String): bool  │ normalise→range→allMatch
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Call chain:
  1. normalise raw
  2. IntStream.range(0, n/2)
  3. allMatch(mirror equality)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To test a palindrome with streams I take the length n and iterate only the first half using IntStream dot range of zero to n over two. For each index i I compare the character at i with its mirror at n minus one minus i, and I wrap that comparison in allMatch, which returns true only if every mirrored pair matches. allMatch short-circuits, so the first mismatch returns false immediately without examining the rest.

I deliberately iterate only half the string, because once the first half matches the mirrored second half the whole string is confirmed, and a single middle character in an odd-length string mirrors itself so it needs no check. This is more efficient than reversing the entire string and comparing, because it allocates nothing and stops early.

The senior point I stress is normalisation. A real palindrome check at the National Bank of India lowercases the input and strips spaces and punctuation before the index comparison, so that phrases and mixed-case codes are judged on their letters alone. The half-range approach also handles the edge cases naturally — empty and single-character strings come out as palindromes — which is exactly the behaviour I want in a validation rule that flags overly predictable reference codes.
